nodes.speaker: mara
nodes.text: Is there a specific interaction where respect made you read practice differently?

nodes.speaker: jules
nodes.text: Can you think of a version of practice that would surprise the rest of us?

nodes.speaker: sarah
nodes.text: I hear Owen leaning on practice; I put more weight on skill, because frustration could make the same situation come out differently.

nodes.speaker: owen
nodes.text: That earlier Mara point lands differently now that skill is part of the thread.

nodes.speaker: mara
nodes.text: For me, frustration gets concrete when it changes what happens between people, especially around skill.

nodes.speaker: jules
nodes.text: What's the strangest case where frustration and skill point in opposite directions?

nodes.speaker: sarah
nodes.text: What interests me in frustration is the point where skill stops predicting it.

nodes.speaker: owen
nodes.text: Mara, earlier in this thread you said “For me, frustration gets concrete when it changes what happens between people, especially around skill.” I think skill gives that a sharper edge now.

nodes.speaker: mara
nodes.text: I keep hearing frustration as a people question: who reacts differently when skill enters the picture?

nodes.speaker: jules
nodes.text: If respect suddenly changed, what unexpected thing would happen to frustration?

nodes.speaker: sarah
nodes.text: Mara's point about frustration and my concern about skill are not quite the same claim; distortion is where I'd compare them.

nodes.speaker: owen
nodes.text: Before I generalize frustration, I'd want to know what happens under the constraint imposed by skill.
